lesson.title: Why does less energy reach the top?

steps.headline: Only part of the energy at one trophic level reaches the next.

lead.text: A trophic level is a feeding step: producers, then the animals that eat them, then their predators.
Organisms use most of their energy to live, and not everything is eaten or digested. The percentage that passes up is the transfer efficiency.

steps.headline: Producers hold 4000 kJ. At 10% transfer, how much energy reaches level 3?

workedSteps.text: Level 2 receives a tenth of the producers' energy.
Level 3 receives a tenth of what level 2 holds.

steps.headline: Producers hold 2000 kJ. At 10% transfer, how much energy reaches level 3?

workedSteps.text: Level 2 receives a tenth of the producers' energy.
Level 3 receives a tenth of what level 2 holds.

steps.headline: 10% is a stated assumption, not a law of nature.

lead.text: Real transfer efficiencies differ between ecosystems, so problems state the figure to use.
A stated 20% passes twice as much energy as 10% from the same starting amount.
This problem states a different efficiency. Use the figure it gives, and apply it to the producers' energy.

reveal.text: You used the stated efficiency. The same method works for any figure, and a higher efficiency passes on more.

lead.text: Now the question runs the other way. The level below must hold more than the level above, by the factor the transfer takes away.

reveal.text: You worked backwards by dividing by the efficiency. Supporting a small amount at a high level takes a much larger amount lower down.

lesson.orientation: Calculate trophic transfers using an explicit efficiency assumption.
lesson.reviewLabel: Why does less energy reach the top?
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A farmer feeds a cow 100 kg of grain. Over the same time the cow gains 10 kg of body mass.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out how much energy reaches each level of a food chain, forwards and backwards, from a stated efficiency.
intro.whyItMatters: It is why food chains are short and why meat needs far more land than plants.

recap.keyIdea: Only a stated fraction of energy passes to the next level, so energy shrinks at every step. Divide by the same fraction to work backwards.

blocks.text: You applied a 10% transfer once and twice, and tried a stated 20%. You also worked back from 300 kJ to 3000 kJ.

recap.nextHook: Populations grow until something stops them. Why can't a population grow forever?

questions.prompt: Producers contain 1000 kJ of energy in the stated accounting. At an assumed 10% transfer, how many kJ reach the next level?
hints: Convert the percentage to a decimal fraction.
Apply the fraction to the producers' energy.
Multiply the producers' energy by one tenth.
questions.onCorrect: 100 kJ. A 10% transfer passes on one tenth of the energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy that does not pass on. The question asks how much reaches the next level.
That multiplies by ten. A percentage below a hundred makes the amount smaller.

questions.prompt: Starting with 2000 kJ, how many kJ reach level 3 after two assumed 10% transfers?
hints: Level 3 is two steps above the producers.
Apply 10% at each step.
Take one tenth of the energy left after the first step.
questions.onCorrect: 20 kJ. Two 10% steps leave 1% of the starting energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 2. One more transfer is needed to reach level 3.
That subtracts a tenth instead of passing on a tenth.

questions.prompt: With 5000 kJ at producers and a 20% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 2?
hints: Use the stated efficiency.
A fifth is the same as 20%.
Take one fifth of the producers' energy.
questions.onCorrect: 1000 kJ. A stated 20% passes on twice as much as 10% would from the same start.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 10% of the producers' energy. This problem states 20%.
That is the energy that does not pass on. Level 2 receives the share that does.

questions.prompt: A next level needs 300 kJ at an assumed 10% transfer. How many kJ are required in the level below?
hints: Work backward through the transfer.
The required output is one tenth of the input.
Divide the required energy by the efficiency as a decimal.
questions.onCorrect: 3000 kJ. Working backwards means dividing by the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the efficiency, which goes forwards. Work backwards by dividing.
That adds a tenth back on. Divide by the efficiency to undo it.

questions.prompt: Does every real food web transfer exactly 10% between levels?
hints: Separate a modelling assumption from a measured law.

acceptedIdeas: No, efficiency varies and must be specified or measured
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ten-percent value is a useful stated approximation, not an exact universal constant.

choices.label: No, efficiency varies and must be specified or measured
No, energy is always fully transferred

questions.onCorrect: No. Efficiency varies between systems, so a problem states the value to use.

misconceptions.feedback: Measured efficiencies differ between ecosystems. 10% is a stated assumption.
Much of the energy is used by the organisms or disperses as heat.

questions.prompt: A fourth level is three steps above producers. From 8000 kJ with an assumed 10% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 4?
hints: Count the number of transfers.
Apply the efficiency once for each transfer.
Track the sequence step by step.
questions.onCorrect: 8 kJ. Three transfers at 10% leave one thousandth of the starting energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 3. One more transfer is needed.
That is the energy at level 2. Two more transfers are needed.

questions.prompt: Level 3 holds 50 kJ and the transfer efficiency is 10%. How many kJ did level 2 hold?
hints: The level below holds more than the level above.
The output is one tenth of the input.
Divide by the efficiency as a decimal.
questions.onCorrect: 500 kJ. Undo a 10% transfer by dividing by the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the efficiency, which goes forwards. Work backwards by dividing.
That adds a tenth back on. Divide to undo the transfer.

questions.prompt: Producers hold 6000 kJ and the transfer efficiency is 10% at each step. How many kJ reach level 3?
hints: Level 3 is two steps above the producers.
Apply the efficiency once for each step.
Take a tenth, then a tenth of that.
questions.onCorrect: 60 kJ. Two transfers at 10% leave a hundredth of the starting energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 2. One more transfer is needed.
That takes a tenth three times. Level 3 needs only two transfers.

questions.prompt: How many kilograms of grain does the farmer feed for each kilogram of body mass the cow gains?
hints: Compare the grain fed with the mass gained.
How many times does the gain fit into the grain?
Divide the grain by the mass gained.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 kg of grain ÷ 10 kg gained = 10 kg of grain per kg gained.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kg of grain for every kg gained. Most of what an animal eats does not become new body mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the amount that did not become body mass. The question asks for grain per kilogram gained.
That adds the grain and the gain. Compare them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Why is the second 10% taken from the energy at level 2 and not from the original amount?
hints: Each transfer moves energy from one level to the next.

acceptedIdeas: Each transfer starts from the energy that reached the level it leaves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The second transfer passes on a share of what level 2 holds.

choices.label: Each transfer starts from the energy that reached the level it leaves
The original amount is no longer counted
Level 2 gains extra energy from the sun

questions.onCorrect: Each step passes on a share of what that level holds, so the shares multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: The original energy is still the source. It has just been reduced by the first transfer.
In this accounting nothing new enters at level 2.

citations.claim: Only some production at one trophic level becomes production at the next; organisms use energy in metabolism.
A transfer percentage applies at each step.
Two 10% transfers leave 1% of the initial energy at the third level.
Transfer efficiency varies between systems; a stated figure is a problem assumption, not a universal law.
A stated 20% transfers more than 10% from the same initial energy.
To support a target amount at a consumer level, divide by the assumed transfer fraction.
The ten-percent value is a useful stated approximation, not an exact universal constant.
Only part of the energy or mass an animal takes in becomes new body mass.
The second transfer passes on a share of what level 2 holds.
